You write cross-sectional factors for Binance USDT perpetual futures, using daily bars.

A factor is one expression that gives every coin a number each day. A higher number means the coin is expected to do better over the following days. You will be given a one-sentence idea; turn it into a factor.

Data, one value per coin per day:
- Factor('open'), Factor('high'), Factor('low'), Factor('close'): prices
- Factor('volume'): amount traded, in units of the coin
- Factor('quote_volume'): amount traded, in USDT
- Factor('num_trades'): number of trades
- Factor('taker_base_vol'), Factor('taker_quote_vol'): the part of volume and of quote_volume that came from aggressive buyers

Operators:
- Arithmetic and comparisons: + - * / ** > >= < <= == != (a comparison gives 1 or 0)
- Each value on its own: .Abs() .ln() .sign() .pow(x) .clip(lower=a, upper=b) .max(other) .min(other) .fillna(other) .safe_div(other), and where(condition, a, b)
- One coin over its past n days, n a positive integer: .ts_mean(window=n, min_periods=m) .ts_std .ts_var .ts_sum .ts_max .ts_min .ts_median .ts_skew .ts_kurt .ts_rank (the latest value's rank in its window, from 1 to n) .ts_zscore .ts_argmax .ts_argmin .ts_decay_linear .ts_product (all take window and min_periods), .ts_quantile(window=n, q=x), .ts_corr(other, window=n), .ts_cov(other, window=n)
- Exponential averages: .EMA(span=n, min_periods=m) .ts_ewm_mean(span=n, min_periods=m)
- Earlier values: .lag(periods=n) .diff(periods=n) .pct_change(periods=n)
- All coins on one day: .sec_rank() .zscore() .demean() .sec_pct() .winsorize(limit=x) .scale() .neutralize(other)

Example: Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=5)) - 1 is each coin's return over the past 5 days.

Every operator only reads the past. Windows and periods must be positive, at most 365.

The factor must be driven by the data the idea talks about and must point the way the idea says: if the idea says something is bearish, the factor must go down when that thing goes up. Values must be comparable across coins, so a coin's price unit must not matter.

Before you answer you can try candidates with the test_factor tool. Give it one expression. It tells you whether the expression computes and, on data from July 2022 to December 2024, its rank IC with the next day's return and its incremental IC, which is what remains after removing liquidity, volatility, short-term reversal and momentum. Higher is better, and an incremental IC of 0.01 to 0.03 is already good.

You may call test_factor at most 5 times, one call per turn. Testing many variants on the same history overfits it, so stop once you have something sound. test_factor does not check that the factor matches the idea; that is up to you. Keep the direction the idea says even if the IC comes out negative: the idea may simply be wrong on this history.

Write Factor('close') with single quotes inside the tool call. When you are done, reply without calling a tool and finish with the factor between <factor> and </factor>. A reply with no factor scores 0.

Idea: Coins with high trading volume are more likely to rise.

**Test 1 — the level reading.** The idea says the amount traded itself is what matters, so the simplest faithful form is the coin's own recent USDT turnover, averaged to smooth daily noise and logged so big and small coins are on one scale. Twenty days with min_periods 16 is my starting window. If this is mostly just "size", the incremental IC should be near zero, since size-like liquidity is already taken out.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0371
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0011 (t = -1.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0025, 2023 -0.0020, 2024 +0.0004

**Test 2 — volume relative to its own normal.** The level form is essentially the size/liquidity style, so its near-zero incremental IC says little about the idea. Reading "high volume" as *unusually high for this coin* strips out permanent size: recent turnover divided by its own longer baseline. Direction stays as the idea says — a higher ratio is more bullish.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0096 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0151, 2023 -0.0150, 2024 -0.0014

**Test 3 — recent level, shorter window.** The ratio form does carry real incremental information (t = −3.3, negative in all three periods), but with the sign opposite to the idea, so it is a worse submission than the near-zero level form. Before settling, one more check in the idea's own form: a 5-day average log turnover, which is closer to "currently trading a lot" and less overlapping with the 30-day size average that is already stripped out.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0440
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0071 (t = -5.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0115, 2023 -0.0085, 2024 -0.0035

That settles it: both follow-up forms are several thousandths worse than the 20-day level (−0.0071 and −0.0096 versus −0.0011), so two tests in a row have failed to beat the best and I stop here.

What I found: the idea does not hold on this history. Ranking coins by log average USDT turnover gives a rank IC of −0.037 — the heavily traded coins actually did slightly worse, not better — and once liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum are stripped out only −0.0011 remains (t = −1.9, and the sign even flips in 2024). Reading "high volume" as unusually high relative to the coin's own baseline makes the reversal clearer and more robust (−0.0096 with t = −3.3, negative in all three sub-periods; and −0.0071 for a 5-day level, t = −5.6), which is the opposite of what the idea predicts. I kept the direction the idea states rather than flipping the sign to chase the higher number, and submit the simplest faithful level reading.

<factor>Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=20, min_periods=16).ln()</factor>

Idea: A coin whose volume has jumped well above its own usual level tends to keep rising.

The idea is about a coin's volume rising *relative to its own normal level*, so the natural measure is a short-window average of USDT-denominated volume divided by a longer baseline of the same coin — this keeps it unit-free and comparable across coins. Direction is positive: the bigger the surge over its own norm, the better the expected return. I'll start with the simplest version, 5 days over 60 days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0096 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0151, 2023 -0.0150, 2024 -0.0014

The simple ratio comes out at −0.0096 incremental IC, consistently negative across all three periods — so on this history a volume surge relative to its own norm is bearish, the opposite of the idea. Before concluding that, I want to check whether the measurement form matters: a surge measured in units of the coin's own volatility (rather than a raw ratio) is the same idea written differently, so I'll test that.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0382
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0112 (t = -4.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0213, 2023 -0.0131, 2024 -0.0043

Same story: −0.0112, still negative in every period and no better than the first form, so the sign isn't an artifact of how I normalize. One last check on the same idea with a shorter, more "sudden jump" framing and medians instead of means, to make sure the result isn't driven by a single spike day.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0297
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0169 (t = -6.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0185, 2023 -0.0193, 2024 -0.0137

That's conclusive in the opposite direction: the more sudden the jump (3-day median over 20-day median), the more negative the incremental IC (−0.0169, t = −6.1), and all three periods point the same way. Two tests in a row failed to improve on my best, so I'll stop testing.

What I found: measured three different ways — a 5/60 mean ratio, a surge in units of the coin's own volatility, and a 3/20 median ratio — a coin's volume rising above its own usual level predicts *lower* returns the next day, with the incremental IC between −0.010 and −0.017 and a consistent sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. So the idea as stated does not hold on this history; the honest reading is that crowded, high-turnover bursts tend to mean-revert rather than continue. Because the direction belongs to the idea and not to the data, I'm keeping it positive (volume surge → higher factor value) and handing in the simplest, best-performing version rather than flipping the sign to chase IC.

<factor>Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4).safe_div(Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=60, min_periods=48))</factor>

Idea: Coins whose price moves more per dollar traded, meaning they are illiquid, earn higher returns.

The idea is an illiquidity premium: how much the price moves per dollar traded. I'll measure it as the log of the absolute daily return divided by USDT turnover, averaged over a few days — a ratio, so it's comparable across coins, and its value rises when price impact per dollar is high. First I'll try the shortest version over a 6-day window.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0293
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0041 (t = 3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0053, 2023 +0.0070, 2024 +0.0006

Rank IC is +0.029 but only +0.0041 survives the style removal, and 2024 is essentially flat — the raw ratio is dominated by a few extreme days for tiny-turnover coins. Next I'll take the cross-sectional rank of each day's ratio before averaging, so a single wild day can't dominate the score, and smooth over 5 days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0289
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0031 (t = 2.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0030, 2023 +0.0049, 2024 +0.0014

Same or slightly worse, so the extreme days were carrying real signal rather than just noise. The bigger problem is that this ratio is basically an inverse-turnover level, which the liquidity style already removes. I'll keep the same quantity (price move per dollar) but express it against the coin's own recent norm — 5-day average impact over 60-day average impact — so it measures unusually high price impact per dollar rather than size.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0349
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0094 (t = 3.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0083, 2023 +0.0123, 2024 +0.0071

Good jump: +0.0094 incremental with t = 3.7 and all three periods positive (0.0083 / 0.0123 / 0.0071). One more refinement: the numerator is currently the raw daily move, which on a market-wide day is inflated for every coin at once and pollutes the "per dollar" ratio. I'll compare each coin's move against the cross-section that day before taking the absolute value, then keep the same short-vs-long structure.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0168
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0017 (t = 0.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0024, 2023 +0.0040, 2024 -0.0011

Much weaker (+0.0017), so the market-common part of the move was doing real work — coins that move a lot per dollar on big market days are the illiquid ones. I'll go back to the winning raw form for my last test and only amplify the extremes inside the average, squaring the daily impact ratio before each average, since the earlier results showed the tail of the distribution carries the signal.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0355
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0100 (t = 3.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0094, 2023 +0.0131, 2024 +0.0072

That is +0.0100 versus +0.0094 — a gain of only 0.0006, well under the 0.002 that would justify the extra operation, and it follows a clear failure, so I'll stop here and take the simpler of the two.

What I found: measuring price impact per dollar (absolute daily return divided by USDT turnover) as a *level* only survives style removal at about +0.004, because its level is largely inverse turnover, which is already accounted for. Expressing the same quantity against the coin's own 60-day norm — recent 5-day impact relative to its usual impact — lifts the incremental IC to +0.0094 (t = 3.7) with the same sign in all three periods (0.0083 / 0.0123 / 0.0071), which supports the idea: coins that have become unusually expensive to move per dollar traded do earn more afterwards. Removing the market-wide move from the numerator destroyed the signal (+0.0017), so the raw move, including market days, is the right measurement.

Idea: Coins with many trades per day tend to do better.

The idea is about the count of trades a coin does per day — a level, and no price unit enters it, so cross-coin comparison is already meaningful once I compress the scale. I'll start with the simplest level reading: average number of trades over a short window, logged so a few huge-count coins don't dominate.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0452
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0071 (t = -5.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0065, 2023 -0.0092, 2024 -0.0052

The level reading has a large raw IC (−0.045), but only −0.007 survives the style removal, which tells me the "many trades" level is mostly a size/liquidity proxy that's already priced out; the sign also says more trades → slightly worse returns, contradicting the idea. Next I'll strip the per-coin size baseline and ask whether a coin having many trades relative to its own norm is what carries information.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0256
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0167 (t = -5.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0247, 2023 -0.0206, 2024 -0.0087

The relative-to-itself reading is much stronger: −0.0167 incremental, consistent in all three sub-periods with t = −5.7, so an unusually high trade count for a coin is a genuinely bearish signal here (the opposite of the idea's claim, which I'll keep and report honestly). One more form to test: counting trades per dollar of turnover, which removes the money-flow size component and isolates trade-count intensity.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0181
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0023 (t = -1.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0021, 2023 +0.0005, 2024 -0.0074

Trades-per-dollar is weak and its sign flips between periods (t = −1.4), so that normalization loses the effect. That is one test without improvement on the best, so I'll spend one more on the same best idea with a longer baseline — a 60-day norm makes a "many trades" reading a cleaner surge measure.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0332
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0108 (t = -3.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0162, 2023 -0.0161, 2024 -0.0027

Two tests in a row (trades-per-dollar, then the 60-day baseline) failed to beat −0.0167, so I stop here. The 20-day baseline version is the one I keep.

What I found: the plain level of trade counts looks impressive raw (rank IC −0.045) but almost all of it is coin size and liquidity, which is already priced out — only −0.007 is incremental. Normalizing each coin's trade count by its own 20-day average leaves a real and very consistent signal (−0.0167 incremental, t = −5.7, negative in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024), but its sign is the opposite of the idea's claim: a coin doing an unusual number of trades underperforms over the next days rather than outperforming. Further normalizations — trades per dollar of turnover, and a longer 60-day baseline — were weak or inconsistent, so the effect is specifically about a short-term surge in trade count relative to the coin's own recent norm. I keep the direction the idea states, so the factor rises with trade count; on this history that means the idea, as stated, does not hold.
